The A–C identifications on collection 14 page 7 are grounded in the spoken transcript. The flattened A–F text box does not establish exact alignment for all remaining letters, so no D–F answer key is invented.
corrections: All seven principles belong together on collection 13 page 2; the stiffness arrow on that page is correct, so no typo warning is introduced.
The local mass/stiffness explanation is present where constrictions are discussed, including collection 14 page 9.
Repeated air-model pages receive complete local explanations instead of relying on notes assigned to a different page.
Collection 13 pages 21 and 22 explain the unchanged source harmonic frequencies and the vowel-specific changes in their amplitudes.
Assigned membrane frequencies are identified as illustrative rather than generalized to every membrane.
The collection 13 phrase-only prompt applies the established spectrogram concept without claiming a supplied recording or inventing a trace.
The rear-/u/ constriction is retained as the taught balanced-effective-influences case, separate from mass-dominated loading at the lips; cancellation is not restricted to single-mass systems.
review.coverageStyle: Each idea records a specific source concept and the zero-based block indices that explain it; line references are inclusive ranges.

teaching.text: **Increasing mass lowers frequency; increasing stiffness raises frequency**, when the other property stays the same. Frequency is the number of complete vibration cycles per second. A heavier moving mass is harder to turn around, while a stiffer spring produces a stronger return toward equilibrium.

**N movable masses have N modes** in the direction being considered. A mode is a coordinated way the whole system vibrates. With two masses, mode 1 moves them together and mode 2 moves them against each other. Higher modes involve more opposing motion between neighbors, so the springs stretch and compress more and the frequency is higher.
The effect of increasing **m, the mass**, depends on how much that part moves in the mode. Adding mass where motion is large lowers the frequency strongly.
children: At a point that stays still throughout the mode, added mass has no effect on that mode’s frequency. The same added mass can therefore affect different modes differently.

teaching.text: The effect of increasing **k, the stiffness**, depends on how much the spring stretches and compresses. Added stiffness has a large effect where that change is large, because it strengthens the restoring action there.
children: Where neighboring parts move together without changing their separation, the spring is hardly stretching. Increasing its stiffness has little effect there.

teaching.text: **The greatest motion and the greatest stretching occur at different locations.** In the standing-wave patterns being compared, a point with no motion can have strongly changing compression around it. A region that moves a long way can have little change in the spacing between its parts.

An ideal **fixed–fixed string** has a still point at both ends. The **base frequency** is its lowest allowed vibration frequency, belonging to mode 1. Its modes fit one, two, three and more half-wave packets into the same length, so their frequencies are whole-number multiples of the base frequency. These multiples are **harmonics**.

An ideal uniform **fixed–free system** has a still end and a freely moving end. Its modes fit one, three, five and more quarter-wave packets, giving **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency. The vocal-tract air resonances are **formants**, labeled F1, F2 and so on; the odd-multiple relation describes the uniform-tube reference.
children: A **node** stays still throughout the cycle, while an **antinode** has the largest back-and-forth movement. A **quarter-wave packet** connects a node to an antinode, or an antinode to a node.

Starting at the fixed node, an odd number of quarter-wave packets ends at an antinode, keeping the free end moving. An even number ends at another node, which would make the free end stay still. Adding two packets at a time preserves the freely moving end, so the allowed counts remain odd.

teaching.text: **Increasing mass and stiffness together does not automatically make their effects cancel.** At a location with no motion but strong compression, extra mass contributes little and extra stiffness raises the frequency. At a location with strong motion but little compression, extra mass lowers the frequency and extra stiffness contributes little.
children: An unchanged frequency would require the two effective changes to balance. Opposite directions alone do not establish that balance.

coverage.idea: Mass and stiffness have opposite directional effects on vibration frequency
N masses give N ordered modes with increasingly opposed neighboring motion
The local mass effect is weighted by motion in the particular mode
The local stiffness effect is weighted by stretching and compression
Displacement maxima and compression maxima alternate spatially
Fixed–fixed half-wave counts produce integer harmonics
Uniform fixed–free quarter-wave counts produce odd-multiple formants
Location prevents automatic cancellation of mass and stiffness effects

teaching.text: A **normal mode** is a coordinated pattern in which the masses keep the same relationship while vibrating at one frequency. A chain with one movable mass has one mode; chains with two through six masses have two through six modes. **N names the number of movable masses**, so the rule is N masses and N independent modes.

**Mode 1 moves the masses in the same direction together.** With two masses, mode 2 moves one against the other. In longer chains, higher modes divide the masses into more groups moving in opposite directions.
children: For three masses in mode 2, the outer masses move against each other while the middle mass stays still. In mode 3, the middle mass moves against the outer two. The mode number identifies the pattern, not a particular mass. The still middle mass remains part of the three-mass system; being still in one mode does not remove it from the mode count.

teaching.text: More opposing motion between neighboring masses means more spring stretching and compression. That gives a stronger restoring effect, so **higher modes vibrate faster within the same chain**. The masses and springs themselves stay the same.
children: The separate-mass chains generally do not have exact whole-number frequency ratios. Their mode-count rule and the harmonic spacing of an ideal continuous string are different properties.

coverage.idea: Each row contains N independent normal modes for N moving masses
Mode numbers distinguish coordinated patterns, including the still middle mass
More opposed neighboring motion increases restoring action and frequency

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** cannot move at either endpoint. Each endpoint is a **node**, a point that stays still throughout a mode. Between two nodes, a section of string moves up and then down; this section is a **half-wave packet**.
**Mode 1 fits one half-wave packet** into the string’s length. Mode 2 fits two packets, with adjacent sections moving in opposite directions. Modes 3, 4 and 5 fit three, four and five packets.
children: The numbered boxes count these spatial sections. More packets fit into the same length by making each packet shorter, while both endpoints remain still.

teaching.text: For this ideal string, the shorter spatial pattern repeats faster. If the lowest frequency is **100 Hz**, mode 2 is 200 Hz and mode 5 is 500 Hz. **Hertz means cycles per second.** The important relation is one, two, three, four and five times the lowest frequency.
children: The lowest frequency is the **fundamental** or base frequency. Its whole-number multiples are harmonics, so both odd and even harmonics are available in the fixed–fixed string.

coverage.idea: Both fixed endpoints are displacement nodes and define half-wave packets
Mode n fits n half-wave packets into the same length
Integer packet counts explain the harmonic frequency ratios

teaching.text: The **same string can vibrate in several modes at once**. Each separate mode has a regular pattern, but the actual displacement at any point is the sum of the movements contributed by all the modes.
children: Contributions in the same direction add together. Contributions in opposite directions partly cancel. Because the modes repeat at different rates, their combined shape keeps changing.

teaching.text: The five modes have frequencies of **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**. They are five consecutive harmonics of the 100 Hz fundamental. Higher modes complete more cycles in the same time; a greater frequency does not mean a greater distance of movement.
A **spectrum** separates the combined motion into its frequency components. Frequency runs horizontally and **amplitude**, the size of each contribution at the measurement point, runs vertically.
children: The marked pickup point measures the motion at one location. Five peaks mean that all five frequencies are present. The peaks have equal heights because the mode strengths were chosen to give equal contributions at that point; equal heights are not a general rule for every vibrating string.

teaching.text: **A single active mode would give one spectral peak.** If only mode 3 were active, the string would still move, but its spectrum would contain the mode 3 frequency instead of all five. The complicated combined motion can therefore be explained by identifying which modes contribute and how much of each is present.

coverage.idea: Superposition adds mode displacements at each location
The five component frequencies are consecutive harmonics
The spectrum separates frequency from amplitude at the pickup
A single active mode produces a single frequency component

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface rather than a one-dimensional string. Its outside edges remain fixed while regions inside rise and fall. A mode describes a coordinated pattern across the entire surface.

The two numbers in a membrane label count its moving regions in the two surface directions. **(1, 1)** has one broad region; **(2, 1)** and **(1, 2)** have two regions divided along different directions.
children: In **(2, 2)**, four regions alternate with their neighbors. In **(3, 1)**, three regions alternate along one direction. The lines separating opposing regions stay still in that mode.

teaching.text: **All five modes can contribute to one motion.** At each position, their displacements add, producing the changing surface in the combined panel. The spectrum at the pickup point identifies the five frequencies in that mixture.
children: The five equal peak heights describe the chosen contributions at that pickup. They do not mean that every point on the membrane moves by the same amount.

teaching.text: The displayed **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** are assigned illustrative frequencies. Their equal spacing lets the separate components be compared, but these values were not calculated as the natural frequencies of this rectangular membrane. The membrane example directly shows spatial modes combining; it does not establish that every membrane has an integer harmonic series.

coverage.idea: A fixed-edge membrane supports modes across a surface
Two-number labels identify moving regions in two spatial directions
The combined surface and spectrum represent five simultaneous components
The displayed harmonic frequencies are assigned illustrative values

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held still at one end while the other end can move. For the string, the fixed bottom is a **node**, and the free top is an **antinode**, a location with the largest back-and-forth movement over a cycle.
children: An antinode does not remain at its highest position. It passes through **equilibrium**, its resting position, and moves to the other side, while a node stays still throughout the cycle.

teaching.text: The lowest mode goes from no motion at the fixed end to maximum motion at the free end. That is **one quarter-wave**. The next allowed modes fit three, five and seven quarter-waves while keeping the same endpoint conditions.
children: With a lowest frequency of 100 Hz, the allowed frequencies are **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**. Mode 2 is the second allowed pattern but the third harmonic: mode number and harmonic multiple are different counts.

teaching.text: **The boundary conditions select the allowed patterns.** An even number of quarter-waves would leave a still point at the free top, so it would not satisfy the free-end condition. Adding two quarter-waves at a time preserves the moving top.
The four modes can occur together. At the free-end pickup, the spectrum has four peaks at the allowed frequencies. Their equal heights reflect equal contributions arranged for this demonstration.
children: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end halves the fundamental relative to a fixed–fixed string. The two displayed demonstrations are separately tuned to the same 100 Hz fundamental, so their equal lowest labels do not isolate the boundary change.

teaching.text: The **air in the vocal tract** is treated as a fixed–free system: constrained near the vocal folds and freely moving at the lips. Its resonant frequencies are called **formants**. In the uniform-tube reference they follow the odd-multiple pattern; changing the tract’s shape changes the formants.

coverage.idea: A node stays still while an antinode has maximal oscillatory motion
Odd quarter-wave counts distinguish mode number from harmonic number
Both endpoint conditions exclude even quarter-wave counts
The spectrum and tuning describe the specific demonstration
Vocal-tract air resonances are formants in a fixed–free reference

teaching.text: A **quarter-wave packet** runs from a node to an antinode, or from an antinode to a node. One packet connects the fixed bottom directly to the freely moving top in mode 1.

The packet counts are **one, three, five and seven** in modes 1 through 4. Adding one packet would switch the top from an antinode to a node. Adding two packets brings it back to an antinode, so the allowed counts stay odd.
children: The numbered stacks count parts of the spatial pattern, not extra strings or separate masses. All four modes occupy the same overall length.

teaching.text: More packets in the same length means a shorter spatial pattern and a higher vibration frequency. For a 100 Hz fundamental, the four frequencies are **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**.
children: The second mode has three quarter-wave packets, so its frequency is three times the first. It is the second allowed mode, even though it uses the third harmonic multiple.

coverage.idea: A quarter-wave packet joins opposite displacement boundary conditions
Odd packet counts preserve a fixed bottom and moving top
Frequency ratios follow packet counts, not consecutive mode labels

teaching.text: The string must have **no motion at the fixed bottom** and **maximum motion at the free top**. A proposed mode is allowed only if it satisfies both conditions throughout its cycle.
Counting the quarter-wave packets gives **one in mode 1, three in mode 2, five in mode 3 and seven in mode 4**. A quarter-wave is the stretch from a node to an antinode or back again.
children: An even packet count would put the wrong endpoint at the top. The extra packets therefore come in pairs, preserving a node at the bottom and an antinode at the top.

teaching.text: The mode frequencies have the same **1 : 3 : 5 : 7** relationship. If the first frequency is 500 Hz, the second is 1,500 Hz and the third is 2,500 Hz. The particular starting number can change; the odd-multiple relationship comes from how the allowed spatial patterns fit.

coverage.idea: Both endpoint conditions constrain each allowed mode
Quarter-wave counting gives odd packet numbers
The spoken 500–1500–2500 example applies the odd-multiple rule

teaching.text: The **vocal tract** is the air passage above the vocal folds. Its air can be modeled as small masses joined by springs. **Mass** represents the air’s inertia, its resistance to changing motion; **stiffness** represents its restoring response to compression.

The simplified tube is **fixed at the glottal end and free at the lip end**. The glottis is the opening between the vocal folds. The closed end constrains back-and-forth air displacement, while the open lips allow strong air motion.
children: The air moves **longitudinally**, along the tube. The masses do not move sideways in the shape of a bent string; neighboring air elements move toward and away from one another along the passage.

teaching.text: **Mode 1 corresponds to F1**, the first formant or lowest air resonance. **Mode 2 corresponds to F2**, the next air resonance. In this uniform-tube reference, mode 2 vibrates three times as fast as mode 1.
children: F1 and F2 belong to two patterns of the same air system. They are not the names of two air particles or two separate passages.

teaching.text: The marked locations are measured from the glottis: **one-third for /a/**, **two-thirds for /i/** and the **lip end for /u/**. A location can move strongly in one mode and compress strongly in another. That difference explains why one constriction can affect two formants differently.

coverage.idea: Air mass and stiffness represent inertia and compression response
Closed glottal and open lip ends constrain longitudinal air motion
F1 and F2 identify ordered resonances of one air system
Vowel constriction markers locate different parts of each mode

teaching.text: A **formant is a resonance of the air in the vocal tract**. The separate rows isolate mode 1 at F1, mode 2 at F2 and mode 3 at F3, so the same air can be examined in different patterns.

The blue elements move **back and forth along the tube**. Where neighboring elements come closer together and then spread apart, their spacing changes: the air **compresses and expands**. That is where the restoring stiffness matters strongly.
children: Where elements travel together while staying about the same distance apart, the air has strong displacement with little compression. Its **moving mass** matters strongly there.

teaching.text: The **closed glottal end** constrains motion and allows strong compression nearby. The **open lip end** allows strong displacement with little compression. The open end is therefore the clearest place to identify mass-dominated motion.

A region can be almost still while air on its two sides moves toward and away from it. **No displacement at that region does not mean no springiness.** The changing spacing around it can be large even though its own back-and-forth travel is small.

coverage.idea: F1, F2 and F3 label separate resonant patterns of the same air
Changing particle spacing distinguishes compression from shared displacement
Closed and open ends have contrasting local motion and compression
A displacement node can have strong surrounding compression

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract made by the tongue or lips. **High and low** describe tongue height; **front, central and back** describe its position along the mouth. These descriptions locate where the air passage is narrowed.

For **/i/ in dean**, the tongue is high and front, and the constriction is near **two-thirds of the distance from the glottis**. For **/a/ in Don**, the constriction is farther back, near **one-third of that distance**.
children: The glottis is the space between the vocal folds. Fractions such as one-third and two-thirds refer to location measured from that end, not to fractions of a frequency.

teaching.text: For **/u/ in dune**, the tongue is high and back and the lips are rounded close together. The lip narrowing acts at the freely moving end of the air column.
children: **/u/ also has a back constriction.** In the comparison being used, its mass and stiffness effects balance and produce little net formant change. That balanced-effects case is different from lip loading: at the lips, strong displacement makes the mass effect dominate, lowering F1 and F2.

teaching.text: **Schwa in done** is the neutral, relatively uniform reference. **Dan** has a low front vowel. The different vowel shapes matter because moving the narrowing changes which parts of the air’s mode patterns are affected.

coverage.idea: Tongue height and front–back position locate constrictions
The /i/ and /a/ constrictions occupy different fractions from the glottis
Lip rounding lowers formants while the taught rear-/u/ constriction illustrates balanced effective influences
Schwa is the reference and different vowel shapes affect local air modes

teaching.text: A **constriction raises both the effective mass and the effective stiffness** of the air in the narrowed region. Bunching air into less space raises its density; squeezing it also increases its restoring response to compression.

**The two increases do not automatically cancel.** Mass matters according to how much the air moves in a particular mode. Stiffness matters according to how much the air compresses and expands. Those are different local properties.

At a region with **large displacement but little compression**, the added moving mass slows the mode. The extra stiffness contributes little because that region is hardly changing its spacing, so the formant falls.

At a region with **little displacement but strong compression**, adding mass has little effect on the mode. Added stiffness strengthens the restoring action where compression is large, so the formant rises.

**The same constriction can lower F1 and raise F2** if its location moves strongly in mode 1 but compresses strongly in mode 2. The outcome follows from the mode at that location, rather than from treating every narrowing as having one fixed frequency effect.

coverage.idea: A constriction increases local effective mass and stiffness
Mass and stiffness act through different local mode properties
Motion-dominated loading lowers a resonance
Compression-dominated stiffening raises a resonance
One location can affect two formants in opposite directions

teaching.text: In **mode 1**, air motion is constrained at the vocal-fold end and grows toward the open lips. Near the closed end, neighboring air elements repeatedly bunch together and spread apart. Near the lips, they travel back and forth with relatively little change in their spacing.

**Displacement and compression are different.** Displacement is how far an air element travels from rest. Compression is a change in spacing between neighboring elements. Several elements can travel a long way together without being squeezed closer together.

Higher modes add more alternating regions of strong motion and strong compression along the same tube. A point with almost no displacement can lie between regions moving toward and away from it, producing strong compression around that point.
children: A still point belongs to the mode pattern. It does not mean that all the surrounding air is stationary.

teaching.text: These local differences determine the effect of a constriction. **Added mass has its strongest effect where air moves; added stiffness has its strongest effect where air compresses.** Comparing those two changes at the actual location gives the direction of the formant change.

coverage.idea: Mode 1 contrasts closed-end compression with open-end displacement
Displacement is distinguished from changing particle spacing
Higher modes add alternating compression and displacement regions
Local motion and compression determine the response to a constriction

teaching.text: **F1, F2 and F3** are the first, second and third resonances of the vocal-tract air. The number orders the resonances from lowest to highest; it does not by itself say that F2 is twice F1.
For the **uniform fixed–free tube**, the allowed patterns fit one, three and five quarter-wave packets. Its first three formants therefore have the relationship **F1, 3 × F1 and 5 × F1**.
children: With an illustrative F1 of **200 Hz**, that gives F2 at **600 Hz** and F3 at **1,000 Hz**. The 200 Hz starting value is an example; actual values depend on the particular tract and air system.

teaching.text: **Schwa** provides an approximately uniform vocal-tract reference. In a measured schwa, formants near **500, 1,400 and 2,500 Hz** were compared with the approximate one, three and five pattern.
children: The comparison tests a prediction about the relationships among resonances. A real measurement can be close to the uniform-tube pattern without reproducing every idealized value exactly.

teaching.text: Changing the tract’s shape places constrictions at particular locations. Those changes affect the modes differently, so the formants of a nonuniform vowel tract are not required to remain exact odd multiples.

coverage.idea: Formant numbers order resonances rather than multiply frequencies
The uniform fixed–free reference gives odd-multiple frequency ratios
A measured schwa provides an approximate empirical test
Constrictions alter the uniform reference differently across modes

teaching.text: **Free-end loading** means adding effective mass near the freely moving lip end. For **/u/**, rounded lips narrow the passage there, increasing both the local effective mass and stiffness.
The lip region has **strong back-and-forth motion in both mode 1 and mode 2**. Neighboring air elements move together there with little compression and expansion.
children: The added mass matters because that air is moving strongly. The increased stiffness matters much less because there is little local compression for it to act on.

teaching.text: **F1 falls and F2 falls.** Extra moving mass makes both modes harder to reverse, so both vibrations slow down. The result follows from what both modes do at the lips, rather than from a rule that every constriction lowers every formant.
A transition from **schwa to /u/** provides a direct comparison in the same voice. The observed first and second formants move downward during lip rounding, matching the free-end-loading prediction.
children: The relevant result is the downward change in both formants. Their exact starting values differ across voices.

coverage.idea: Lip rounding introduces free-end loading in the /u/ model
Both first modes have strong lip motion and little compression
Local mass loading slows both F1 and F2
A same-voice schwa-to-/u/ measurement supports the prediction

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two-thirds of the distance from the glottis**. It is the same physical location in the two mode rows, but the air behaves differently there in each mode.
In **mode 1**, the air at that location moves strongly back and forth with little compression. The constriction adds effective mass to a moving region, so the vibration slows and **F1 falls**.
In **mode 2**, the air at that location compresses and expands strongly. The constriction increases stiffness where stiffness matters, strengthening the restoring action, so **F2 rises**.
children: Both mass and stiffness increase under the one constriction. Their effects do not cancel because displacement dominates one mode locally and compression dominates the other.

teaching.text: The predicted combination is **low F1 and high F2**. A measured transition from schwa into /i/ shows the first formant dropping and the second rising. That opposite movement is evidence for the local-mode explanation.
The vocal folds supply the vibration, and the air above them has its own resonances. Changing the tongue’s position changes those air resonances, allowing the same voice to produce a different vowel.
children: Vocal-fold vibration moves the air, and the resulting sound reaches vibrating structures in the **listener’s ear**. Their response also depends on **mass and stiffness**.

coverage.idea: The /i/ narrowing acts at one location in both mode patterns
Motion-dominated loading lowers F1
Compression-dominated stiffening raises F2
Measured opposite formant movements match the prediction
Tongue position changes air resonances while the voice supplies excitation
The sound-production chain continues through air to the listener’s vibrating ear structures

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is farther back, near **one-third of the distance from the glottis**. Moving the constriction changes which local part of each mode is affected.
In **mode 1**, compression and expansion are strong in that back region. Increasing stiffness strengthens the restoring action there, so the first resonance speeds up and **F1 rises**.
In **mode 2**, the same region has stronger back-and-forth air motion. Increasing effective mass makes the motion harder to reverse, so the second resonance slows and **F2 falls**.

The combination is **higher F1 and lower F2**, the reverse of the /i/ comparison. The mass and stiffness rules stay the same; the constriction has moved to a location where the two modes have different local behavior.
children: A single tract narrowing can therefore move two formants toward one another, just as another narrowing can move them apart.

coverage.idea: The /a/ constriction is near one-third from the glottis
Local stiffness dominance raises the first formant
Local displacement dominance lowers the second formant
Changing the constriction location reverses the /i/ pattern

teaching.text: The **same air column has several resonant modes**. Mode 1 at F1, mode 2 at F2 and mode 3 at F3 differ in their patterns of displacement and compression, rather than representing three different air passages.
In mode 1, there is one displacement node at the closed end. Mode 2 has that node and an additional internal node; mode 3 has two internal nodes in addition to the closed-end node.
children: A **node** stays still throughout the cycle. A moving air element passing through its resting position for an instant is not a node.

teaching.text: Around a node, air on neighboring sides can move toward and away from it. The spacing changes strongly there, producing **compression and expansion despite little local displacement**.

Between those regions, air can travel together with much less spacing change. **Higher modes repeat this alternation more times along the same tract.** The movement at the exact constriction location determines which formant responds strongly to extra mass or extra stiffness.

coverage.idea: Several air modes belong to one physical air column
Higher modes have more displacement nodes
Compression can be strong around a displacement node
Alternating regions determine local constriction effects

teaching.text: **Source–filter theory** combines two vibrating systems. The **source** is the glottal vibration of the vocal folds, which supplies harmonics. The **filter** is the air in the vocal tract, whose resonances are the formants.

The source spectrum has evenly spaced harmonic lines. In this example they are **100 Hz apart**. Passing through the tract changes each harmonic’s **amplitude**, its height in the spectrum, according to how close it lies to a formant.
children: Harmonics near a formant are stronger; harmonics far from the formants are weaker. The filter shapes existing source frequencies instead of creating an extra harmonic at each formant.

teaching.text: For **schwa**, the formant targets are approximately **500, 1,500, 2,500 and 3,500 Hz** in this example. The filtered spectrum has groups of tall harmonic lines near those targets and lower lines between them.

**The harmonic frequencies stay in the same places while their heights change.** The source controls the spacing between the narrow lines; the tract’s formants control the broad pattern of tall and short lines.
children: The **spectral envelope** is the outline across the harmonic heights. Its broad peaks reveal the vowel’s formant pattern, while the individual narrow peaks remain harmonics of the source.

coverage.idea: The source supplies harmonics and the tract supplies formant resonances
The filter changes amplitudes of existing harmonics
The schwa example favors harmonics near odd-multiple formant targets
Fixed harmonic locations and a changing spectral envelope separate source from filter

teaching.text: The **/i/ filter** has a low first formant and a high second formant. The example marks **F1 at 300 Hz and F2 at 2,300 Hz**. These are the air resonances favored by this vowel shape, not the source’s fundamental frequency.

The **same source supplies harmonic lines every 100 Hz**. The /i/ tract makes the lines near F1 and F2 strong and leaves many lines between them weak. That produces a low cluster of tall peaks, a wide quieter region and another cluster near the higher F2.

**The filter changes harmonic amplitudes, not their frequency locations.** A line at 100, 200 or 300 Hz remains at that frequency; its height can change. Moving the formants changes which of the existing source harmonics receive the strongest response.
The higher marked resonances, **F3 and F4**, are the third and fourth formants. Together with F1 and F2 they shape the broad **spectral envelope**, the outline across the harmonic heights.
children: The vowel is identified by this pattern of resonances and strengths. The large gap between F1 and F2 is the central /i/ feature in this comparison.

coverage.idea: The /i/ example places F1 low and F2 high
The unchanged 100 Hz source is shaped into separated strong harmonic groups
Filtering changes amplitudes while retaining source harmonic frequencies
Higher formants contribute to the vowel envelope

teaching.text: The **/a/ filter** brings the first two formants closer together. The example marks **F1 at 750 Hz and F2 at 1,200 Hz**, giving a higher F1 and lower F2 than the /i/ example.

The source still provides **harmonics every 100 Hz**. The tract favors the existing harmonics near its formant targets, so strong lines gather into a lower, more closely grouped region instead of the widely separated F1 and F2 groups of /i/.

**The same harmonic frequencies can carry different vowels.** Changing the filter changes the heights of the lines, while the lines remain at the source frequencies. A formant between two harmonics can strengthen neighboring harmonics without adding a new source line at the formant frequency.
children: For example, the 750 Hz formant lies between source harmonics at 700 and 800 Hz. Those neighboring source frequencies can be strengthened without creating a new harmonic at 750 Hz.

teaching.text: The broad **spectral envelope** follows the strengths of those lines. Its peaks reflect F1, F2 and the higher formants, while the narrow individual peaks reflect the harmonics. This separates the vowel’s tract resonances from the vibration rate of the voice.

coverage.idea: The /a/ example raises F1 and lowers F2 relative to /i/
An unchanged source is reshaped into closer formant groups
Changing the filter changes harmonic amplitudes without moving frequencies
The envelope identifies tract resonances while narrow peaks identify harmonics

teaching.text: A **spectrum** describes one short instant of sound. Its horizontal axis is frequency and its vertical axis is amplitude. Speech changes as the tongue and lips move, so a single spectrum cannot show the whole change.

A **spectrogram** places successive spectra along time. **Time runs horizontally, frequency runs vertically and darkness represents amplitude.** A dark area contains stronger energy at that frequency and moment; a pale area contains less.
children: Tall spectral peaks become dark marks at their frequency positions. Repeating this through time makes the stronger resonant regions appear as bands.

teaching.text: During **/i/**, F1 is low and F2 is high, so the two formant bands are far apart. As the sound changes into **/a/**, the low band rises and the higher band falls: **F1 rises and F2 falls**.
children: The moving dark bands track changing formants. Their changing positions come from changing vocal-tract shape, while the spectrogram preserves when those changes occur.

coverage.idea: A spectrum captures frequency and amplitude at one instant
A spectrogram adds time and encodes amplitude as darkness
The /ia/ example brings the first two formant bands together

teaching.text: **“Where were you a year ago?” is connected speech that changes over time.** Producing the phrase involves moving between sounds, so the tongue and lips keep changing the air passage rather than holding one vowel shape throughout.
A **spectrogram** can show those changing resonances across the phrase. Time locates each part of the utterance, frequency locates the formant bands and darkness indicates the strength of the sound.
children: A spectral slice describes one moment. Following the bands across time is what reveals how the vocal-tract resonances develop through connected speech.

coverage.idea: The written phrase applies time-varying tract shape to connected speech
Spectrogram axes support following formants through a whole phrase

teaching.text: **Formants are revealed by how they shape the source harmonics.** When harmonics are closely spaced, many lines fall around each resonance, so their changing heights trace the formant envelope clearly.
The example begins with harmonics at **100, 200, 300 and 400 Hz**, with F1 near **300 Hz** and F2 near **2,100 Hz**. Many harmonic lines are available around both resonances.
children: Increasing the harmonic spacing to **250 Hz** leaves fewer lines in the same frequency range. A formant can fall between those lines, making its location less obvious in the measured spectrum.

teaching.text: **Raising F0 spaces harmonics farther apart; it does not by itself move the formants.** Holding the vowel filter fixed can therefore give a smooth-looking spectrum at low F0 and a sparse, ambiguous-looking spectrum at high F0.

A toddler’s harmonics can be spaced by about **400 Hz**, while a soprano’s can be spaced by about **800 Hz**. Those wider intervals make the formant pattern harder to recover from the available harmonic peaks.
children: The difficulty is identifying the tract’s broad resonances from a smaller set of source frequencies. A tall isolated harmonic is not automatically the exact location of a formant.

coverage.idea: Dense harmonic spacing reveals the formant envelope
The 100 Hz and 250 Hz examples differ in how many harmonics sample resonances
F0 changes sampling while the vowel filter can remain fixed
High-pitched voice examples make formant identification harder

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** form one of the two major vibrating systems involved in voiced speech. They are a membrane held around its edges. Different regions can move together or against one another while the outside edges remain constrained.

A **membrane mode** is a coordinated movement pattern across that surface. **(1, 1)** has one broad moving region. **(2, 1)** and **(1, 2)** divide the motion into two opposing regions along different directions.
children: The **(2, 2)** pattern has four alternating regions, and **(3, 1)** has three regions along one direction. These numbers describe the spatial divisions of one surface, not separate membranes.

teaching.text: The combined surface adds all five mode movements at each point. Where their contributions agree, the displacement is larger; where they oppose one another, the contributions partly cancel. The result changes shape even though each component has a regular pattern.

The spectrum at the pickup has five component peaks. The displayed **100 to 500 Hz** are assigned harmonic frequencies for this illustration, and the equal peak heights are arranged at the pickup. They are not a calculation of the natural frequencies of every rectangular membrane.

For the voiced source, the lowest harmonic is called **F0**, and the other harmonics occur at multiples of that fundamental. Different voices can have different F0 values while retaining that regular spacing. **F0 describes the source**, while F1 and F2 describe resonances of the air above the vocal folds.

coverage.idea: The fixed-edge vocal folds provide a vibrating membrane source
Two-number labels identify membrane spatial patterns
Mode displacements add into a combined moving surface
Assigned illustrative frequencies and pickup amplitudes describe this demonstration
F0 is the voice fundamental and differs from vocal-tract formants

teaching.text: A string with **one fixed end and one free end** must remain still at the fixed bottom while allowing maximum oscillatory motion at the top. The bottom is a **node** and the top is an **antinode**.
The first mode goes from that still bottom to the moving top in one **quarter-wave**. The next allowed modes fit three, five and seven quarter-waves into the same length.
children: Those counts give frequencies at **one, three, five and seven times the fundamental**. For the displayed 100 Hz fundamental, the four frequencies are 100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz.

teaching.text: An even quarter-wave count would end with a node at the top, which conflicts with the freely moving end. **The endpoints decide which patterns are possible.** The second allowed mode is therefore the third harmonic multiple.
When all four modes contribute, their spectrum has peaks at those four frequencies. The equal peak heights reflect the chosen contributions at the free-end measurement point.
children: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end halves the lowest frequency relative to a fixed–fixed string. Matching the lowest frequency across the two demonstrations requires separate tuning.

coverage.idea: Fixed and free boundaries require a node and antinode
Odd quarter-wave counts give the displayed frequency ratios
Endpoint constraints explain skipped even multiples
The spectrum and tuning characterize the particular demonstration

teaching.text: A **quarter-wave packet** connects a point of no movement with a point of largest movement. Mode 1 contains one packet from the fixed bottom to the free top.
The numbered stacks show **three packets for mode 2, five for mode 3 and seven for mode 4**. Adding one packet would reverse the condition at the top; adding two preserves the required antinode.
children: The packets occupy progressively shorter parts of the same string. More packets mean a shorter spatial pattern and a faster repetition rate.

teaching.text: The allowed frequencies therefore follow **1 : 3 : 5 : 7**. The counts name quarter-wave sections of each whole-system pattern. They do not mean that the second mode has a second, separate string or that its frequency must be twice mode 1.

coverage.idea: Quarter-wave packets connect a node and antinode
Paired additions preserve the free end while shortening spatial patterns
Odd frequency ratios follow the allowed packet counts

teaching.text: The **air in the vocal tract** is the second vibrating system. The passage can be treated as a tube extending from the vocal folds through the mouth to the lips. Its walls are formed by the surrounding tongue, palate and throat.
The idealized tube is **closed at the glottis and open at the lips**. Air displacement is constrained at the closed end, while air can oscillate back and forth at the open end.
children: This is longitudinal motion: the air moves along the passage. Compression occurs when neighboring portions move closer together, and expansion occurs when they separate.

teaching.text: In the mass–spring model, **mass represents air’s inertia** and **stiffness represents its restoring response to compression**. The masses and springs describe two properties of the air, rather than objects inserted into the tract.
**Mode 1 gives F1**, the lowest air resonance, and **mode 2 gives F2**, the next one. In the uniform fixed–free reference, mode 2 is three times as fast as mode 1.
children: The markers locate **/a/ near one-third**, **/i/ near two-thirds** and **/u/ at the lips**, measured from the glottis. What each mode does at the marked place determines the effect of narrowing it.

coverage.idea: The vocal tract supplies a second vibrating system of air
Closed and open ends constrain longitudinal motion
Mass and stiffness model air inertia and compression response
F1/F2 and vowel markers identify mode frequencies and locations

teaching.text: **Air displacement and air compression describe different changes.** Displacement is back-and-forth movement from a resting position. Compression is a reduction in the spacing between neighboring air elements, alternating with expansion.

Where neighboring elements move together while keeping about the same spacing, the air acts mainly as a **moving mass**. Where the elements repeatedly bunch together and spread apart, the air acts strongly through its **springiness**.
children: Near a displacement node, one location can remain almost still while air on either side moves toward and away from it. That region can have strong compression despite little displacement.

teaching.text: In **mode 1**, the closed glottal end has constrained motion and strong compression nearby. The freely moving lip end has large displacement with little compression. In higher modes, more regions of displacement and compression alternate along the same tract.

**A constriction must be evaluated within the particular mode.** Added effective mass has a large effect where air moves strongly. Added stiffness has a large effect where compression changes strongly. A fixed location can therefore have different effects on F1, F2 and F3.

coverage.idea: Displacement and compression are distinct physical changes
Shared motion and changing spacing separate mass and spring behavior
Mode 1 and higher modes distribute motion and compression differently
The local mode determines sensitivity to mass and stiffness

teaching.text: The marked locations identify different parts of an **air-mode pattern**. A region dominated by springiness has strong repeated compression and expansion; a region dominated by moving mass has strong back-and-forth displacement with relatively little change in spacing.

At **A**, the air is strongly springy. **B** is dominated by moving mass. At **C**, neighboring air regions bunch together and expand while the marked location moves very little, so C is also strongly springy.
children: A motionless location does not imply that the air around it is inactive. Neighboring elements can change their spacing strongly there.

teaching.text: For the **third mode**, constricting at **C** increases both effective mass and stiffness. The extra mass has little effect because local displacement is small. The extra stiffness strengthens a region that is already compressing and expanding strongly, so **F3 rises**.

The prediction follows from the local movement, rather than from the letter attached to the location. At a different place in the same mode, or the same place in a different mode, the relative importance of mass and stiffness can change.

coverage.idea: Marked regions are identified by displacement versus changing spacing
A and C are spring-dominated while B is mass-dominated
Constriction at C raises F3 because stiffness matters locally
Local patterns determine predictions at other locations

teaching.text: A **constriction** narrows the air passage. The MRI views locate that narrowing within the actual tongue, lips and throat. **High/low** describes tongue height and **front/back** describes how far forward the tongue lies.
**Dean** has a high front vowel, with a constriction near **two-thirds of the distance from the glottis**. **Don** has a low back vowel, with a constriction near **one-third of that distance**.
children: The glottis is the opening between the vocal folds. These fractions locate the constriction along the tract; they are not frequency ratios.

teaching.text: **Dune** has a high back vowel with **lip rounding**, so its important free-end loading occurs at the lips. **Done**, containing schwa, is the neutral, relatively uniform reference. **Dan** has a low front vowel.

The vowel shape determines **where effective mass and stiffness increase**. The same kind of narrowing can lower one resonance and raise another because the air’s motion and compression differ between modes at that place.

coverage.idea: MRI views connect tongue and lip shape with constriction location
The /i/ and /a/ constrictions lie at different tract fractions
The five example words locate different vowel shapes
Tract shape selects the region changed within each air mode

teaching.text: **Constriction increases both effective mass and stiffness.** Narrowing the passage bunches air into less space, increasing its effective density. It also increases the restoring response when that region compresses and expands.

**The two changes do not automatically cancel**, because they act through different local features of a mode. Added mass matters where air has back-and-forth motion. Added stiffness matters where neighboring air portions repeatedly compress and expand.
At a region with **strong displacement and little compression**, added mass slows the vibration, while extra stiffness contributes little. The relevant formant **falls**.
At a region with **little displacement and strong compression**, added mass contributes little, while added stiffness strengthens the restoring action. The relevant formant **rises**.

The places with greatest movement alternate with the places with greatest compression. **One narrowing can therefore move two formants in opposite directions** when the same location is motion-dominated in one mode and compression-dominated in another.

coverage.idea: Narrowing changes local effective mass and stiffness
Different local influences prevent automatic cancellation of mass and stiffness changes
Motion-dominated narrowing lowers a formant
Compression-dominated narrowing raises a formant
Spatial alternation allows opposite effects across modes

teaching.text: The highlighted tract location is **the same physical place in mode 1 and mode 2**. The two rows isolate different ways the same air can move, so they can show different local behavior at that one location.

**F1 is the frequency of mode 1, and F2 is the frequency of mode 2.** For the uniform reference, F2 is three times F1. A constriction changes the reference by making selected air elements effectively heavier and their restoring stiffness greater.

To determine the effect on either formant, the relevant distinction is **motion versus compression at the constriction**. Strong back-and-forth motion makes the added mass important; strong changes in spacing make the added stiffness important.
children: A narrowing near the /i/ location can lower F1 because mode 1 moves there, while raising F2 because mode 2 compresses there. Both effects come from the same constriction.

teaching.text: At the open lips, both modes have strong displacement, so local mass loading lowers both frequencies. Moving the narrowing toward the back changes the local pattern again, allowing F1 to rise while F2 falls.

coverage.idea: Two mode rows show the same tract location participating differently
F1 and F2 identify mode frequencies of one air system
The local motion/compression distinction explains opposite formant changes
Lip and back constrictions have different mode-dependent effects

teaching.text: For **/u/**, rounding the lips narrows the passage at the **free end**. This is **free-end loading**: the air near the lips becomes effectively heavier, while its stiffness also increases.
At the open end, the air travels back and forth strongly in **both mode 1 and mode 2**. Neighboring portions move together with little local squeezing or expansion.
children: The added effective mass therefore matters in both modes. The extra stiffness contributes little because local compression is small.

teaching.text: More moving mass makes each mode harder to turn around. Both modes slow, giving **F1 down and F2 down**. This is a prediction from the local motion of the air, rather than a separate memorized rule about the vowel.
A measured **schwa-to-/u/** transition shows the formants moving downward. The first formant can lie far below the schwa reference, consistent with the heavier moving air at the lips.
children: Exact frequencies vary across voices. The relevant comparison is the change within a voice as the lips round.

coverage.idea: Lip rounding adds effective mass and stiffness at the free end
Both modes have strong lip displacement with little compression
Mass dominance slows both first resonances
Measured formant lowering supports the free-end-loading prediction

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** is near **two-thirds of the distance from the closed glottal end**. The tongue narrows one region, so both local effective mass and stiffness increase there.
In **mode 1**, the air at that region mostly moves back and forth. Added mass therefore has the stronger effect, making the mode slower and **lowering F1**.
In **mode 2**, the air at the same region mostly compresses and expands. Added stiffness has the stronger effect, making the restoring action faster and **raising F2**.
The combined result is **low F1 and high F2**. The opposite directions do not require two separate constrictions; they result from one location participating differently in the two modes.
children: A measured transition from schwa into /i/ shows F1 dropping and F2 rising, matching this prediction.

coverage.idea: The /i/ narrowing is located two-thirds from the glottis
Mode 1 displacement makes added mass lower F1
Mode 2 compression makes added stiffness raise F2
One constriction explains measured opposite changes in two formants

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** lies farther back, near **one-third of the distance from the glottis**. It affects a different part of the air’s mode patterns from the front constriction for /i/.
In **mode 1**, that back region has strong compression and expansion. More stiffness strengthens the restoring action, so the vibration speeds up and **F1 rises**.
In **mode 2**, the constriction falls in a region with stronger back-and-forth air displacement, between strongly compressing regions. Added moving mass slows that pattern, so **F2 falls**.
**Higher F1 and lower F2** bring the two resonances closer together. Measurements of /a/ show that same pattern, with the second formant not far above the first.
children: The result reverses /i/ because the constriction has moved, while the rules connecting moving mass, restoring stiffness and frequency stay the same.

coverage.idea: The /a/ constriction is near one-third from the glottis
Compression dominance raises F1
Motion dominance lowers F2
Measured /a/ formants converge in the predicted direction

teaching.text: The separate **mode 1, mode 2 and mode 3** rows isolate resonant patterns of the same air in the same tract. Their frequencies are called **F1, F2 and F3**.

Each pattern alternates between regions of **large displacement** and regions of **large compression changes**. Air elements that keep similar spacing while traveling together are showing strong mass motion. Elements that bunch together and spread apart are showing strong springiness.
The closed end remains a displacement node, and the open lip end allows strong movement. Higher modes add internal nodes and more alternating regions within that same length.
children: A point staying still throughout a mode is a node. Briefly crossing the resting position during a cycle does not make a moving point a node.

teaching.text: **The location and the mode must both be specified** when explaining a constriction’s effect. Added mass slows modes that move strongly there. Added stiffness speeds modes that compress strongly there. This is why identical physical narrowing can affect F1 and F2 differently.

coverage.idea: The rows isolate three resonant modes of one air column
Spacing changes distinguish compression from shared displacement
Boundary nodes persist while higher modes add internal nodes
Mode-specific local behavior predicts constriction effects

teaching.text: **F0 is the fundamental frequency of the vocal-fold source.** The harmonics occur at multiples of F0. In one example F0 is 100 Hz, giving harmonics at 100, 200 and 300 Hz; at F0 of 250 Hz, the first harmonics are 250, 500 and 750 Hz.
**Mass and stiffness affect F0.** Heavier, looser vocal folds have greater moving mass and less restoring stiffness, which favors a lower F0. Lighter, tighter folds favor a higher F0.
children: A higher F0 gives fewer, more widely separated harmonic lines within the same frequency range. The 350 Hz example therefore has wider spacing than the 100 Hz example.

teaching.text: F0 also changes **within a voice during speech**. Muscles alter vocal-fold stiffness, changing the repetition rate of the source. These pitch changes can contribute to how an utterance is understood.

In **“The dog slept here”** and **“The dog slept here?”**, the same words can have different F0 contours. A falling ending supports the statement pattern in the example, while a rising ending supports the question pattern.
children: The distinction concerns changes in the source frequency, rather than a change from F1 to F2. F1 and F2 are separate air resonances that shape the harmonics.

coverage.idea: F0 sets source harmonic frequencies and spacing
Vocal-fold mass and stiffness affect the fundamental
Muscle control changes F0 within an utterance
Statement/question pitch contours illustrate source-frequency variation

teaching.text: The **vocal-tract filter** is the shaped air passage above the vocal folds. Its resonances are **formants**. They depend on the tract’s shape and the local mass and stiffness of its air, rather than being the same thing as the source’s F0.

For the **schwa reference**, the first two targets are about **500 and 1,500 Hz**. The /u/ targets are lower, **/i/** has a low F1 and high F2, and **/a/** brings F1 and F2 closer together. The locations of the constrictions explain these different patterns.
children: These are **reference values**. The actual formants vary with **vocal-tract length** and the air’s mass and stiffness.

teaching.text: **A formant favors nearby harmonics.** A source harmonic close to a formant becomes strong in the output; harmonics farther away become weaker. The filter changes how much of each available source frequency is transmitted.
children: The filter does not add a new harmonic at every formant. If a formant lies between harmonic lines, the neighboring available harmonics carry the effect.

teaching.text: The narrow harmonic lines identify the source frequencies. The broad pattern of their strengths reveals the **spectral envelope**, which reflects the vowel filter. **Source spacing and filter shape describe different properties of the same sound.**

coverage.idea: The filter supplies formant resonances distinct from F0
Vowel targets reflect different constriction locations
Formants strengthen nearby existing source harmonics
Harmonic spacing and spectral-envelope shape separate source and filter
Schwa reference formants vary with vocal-tract length and air properties

teaching.text: The grid holds **one vowel filter fixed within each column** and changes the source F0 across the rows. The formant targets mark the same resonances down a column; the harmonic frequencies become more widely spaced from the 100 Hz row to the 250 Hz and 350 Hz rows.
With **dense harmonics**, many source lines fall around each formant. Their different heights trace the broad resonant peak clearly, so the formant envelope is easier to identify.

With **sparse harmonics**, few lines fall near a formant, and a target can lie between the available frequencies. The spectrum can therefore make the resonance look weak or ambiguous even though the vowel filter has not changed.
children: Changing F0 changes where the source samples the filter. It does not by itself require the tract’s formants to move.

teaching.text: **High-pitched singing and small children’s voices** illustrate the same difficulty. Wider harmonic spacing leaves less information about the broad resonances, making some vowels harder to distinguish or their formants harder to locate.
children: Changing mouth shape can bring a resonance closer to an available harmonic. That changes the filter to improve its alignment with the source.

teaching.text: A **spectral slice in Praat** can show the harmonics at one moment. The lowest harmonic gives F0, and the spacing to the next harmonics checks that source pattern. A formant is identified from the envelope of harmonic strengths rather than by assuming the tallest individual line is itself a resonance.

coverage.idea: Rows change F0 while columns retain one filter
Dense harmonics trace broad resonances clearly
Sparse sampling can hide a fixed formant
High-pitched voices make source/filter mismatch practically important
A spectral slice distinguishes the source fundamental from filter resonances

teaching.text: A **spectrum** has frequency on one axis and amplitude on the other, describing a short instant. A **spectrogram** arranges many such instants across time so the changing speech sound can be followed.

In a spectrogram, **time runs horizontally**, **frequency runs vertically** and **amplitude becomes darkness**. Stronger energy is darker; weaker energy is lighter. The strong frequency regions form bands as time progresses.
For **/i/**, F1 is low and F2 is high, so the first two bands are far apart. Moving toward **/a/** raises F1 and lowers F2, bringing the bands closer.
children: The band trajectories describe changing vocal-tract resonances. They are not air particles traveling up or down the frequency axis; the air itself oscillates along the tract while the measured resonant frequencies change.

coverage.idea: A spectrogram adds temporal development to successive spectra
Time, frequency and darkness encode three different quantities
The /ia/ transition brings F1 and F2 toward one another

teaching.text: **“Where were you a year ago?” changes its sound continuously.** A spectrogram of the phrase places successive moments along the time axis, frequencies vertically and stronger energy in darker regions.

During **/i/-like portions**, the example shows a high F2 together with a low F1. A constriction in the front region increases stiffness where mode 2 compresses and adds mass where mode 1 moves, explaining those separated resonances.
During the **/u/ portion in “you,”** the formants move downward. Lip rounding loads the moving free end, which lowers the relevant air resonances.
children: Across the phrase, the bands keep changing as the tongue and lips move between sounds. Reading the formant paths therefore explains a sequence of changing tract shapes rather than one steady vowel.

coverage.idea: The phrase spectrogram encodes connected speech through time
High F2 and low F1 identify the /i/-like portions of the spoken example
The /u/ portion shows downward-moving formants from lip loading

teaching.text: A speaker produces **“ma” and “na.”** The **m portion from “ma”** is combined with the **a portion from “na.”** Although the copied consonant comes from “ma,” listeners hear the combined result as **“na.”**

The following vowel contains information about the consonant. In the example, the **a after m** has a relatively stationary formant, while the **a after n** contains a pronounced downward formant movement.
children: That change is in a **formant of the vocal-tract air**, rather than the source F0. Carrying the vowel from “na” into the splice carries the cue that supports hearing n.

teaching.text: **Speech perception combines information across time.** A listener’s consonant decision can depend strongly on the vowel that follows, so interpreting one isolated slice and assigning it a final sound label misses important information.

A speech-recognition system must therefore use relationships across a stretch of sound. The experiment demonstrates why recognizing speech requires temporal context, rather than a separate irreversible decision about every small acoustic piece.

coverage.idea: The ma/na splice combines m with the following vowel from na but is heard as na
A falling vowel formant carries a cue to the preceding n
Consonant perception integrates information from later vowel portions
Speech recognition requires temporal context

teaching.text: A **neural network can use formants to decide which vowel was spoken**. Each recording supplies two input numbers: **F1**, the first air resonance, and **F2**, the second air resonance.

Different vowels produce different combinations of those two measurements. A **low F1 and high F2** supports an /i/ response such as **dean**. The input numbers describe the recording; the output identifies a vowel category.
The network’s **weights, written W**, determine how it turns the input numbers into a decision. **Learning changes the weights** using examples paired with their correct vowel labels.
children: A network that has only random starting weights can process the inputs and still give a poor answer. Performing a calculation and having learned a useful vowel decision are different achievements.

coverage.idea: F1 and F2 serve as measured inputs to vowel recognition
A formant combination supports a vowel-category decision
Learned weights determine how the measurements are interpreted

teaching.text: The network has **two input neurons**, one for F1 and one for F2. A neuron here is a numerical processing unit. The input units receive the measurements and pass them onward.

The three **hidden layers** have **3, 2 and 4 neurons**. They are hidden because they lie between the inputs and the final outputs. Each layer produces a new set of activations, the numbers passed to the following layer.
The network is **fully connected**: every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next. Each connection has a **weight**, which determines the contribution of its incoming value.

An **inner product** multiplies each incoming value by its connection weight and adds the results. Each processing neuron uses this operation to produce its activity. This version is **purely linear**, with no activation function inserted between the hidden layers.
The **five output neurons** correspond to **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**. The network maps one pair of formants through the hidden layers into a decision among those five vowel categories.
children: There are five layers when the input layer is counted: one input layer, three hidden layers and one output layer. The input layer receives values rather than performing the weighted processing.

coverage.idea: Two input neurons receive the formant measurements
Hidden widths 3–2–4 describe successive activation sets
Fully connected layers assign a weight to every next-layer connection
Inner products perform the purely linear processing
Five output categories and five counted layers explain the architecture

teaching.text: The example input is **F1 = 320 Hz and F2 = 2,000 Hz**. Its low F1 and high F2 have the /i/ pattern, so a useful network should favor **dean**.
Every connection has a **random starting weight**, a positive or negative number. These weights are the network’s adjustable knowledge, and a random initial set is not yet tuned to the vowel task.

Each neuron multiplies its incoming values by their own weights and adds the results. A **positive weight** preserves an incoming contribution’s sign; a **negative weight** reverses it. With the positive formant inputs, positive and negative weights therefore contribute in opposite directions.
children: The first processing layer combines two inputs into three activations. Those activations become the inputs used by the following layer. The weight values can change the decision because they change these contributions.

teaching.text: **Inputs describe a recording; weights describe how it is processed.** Supplying a different recording changes F1 and F2. Training changes the weights so that the same kinds of recordings lead to better vowel decisions.

coverage.idea: The 320/2000 Hz input supports the /i/ vowel pattern
Random signed starting weights are untrained parameters
Weighted multiplication and addition produce each layer’s activities
Input values and learned weights have different roles

teaching.text: In **forward propagation**, the formant input moves through the network one layer at a time. Each layer combines incoming activations with its weights and produces the activities supplied to the following layer.
The final display is a **probability distribution over five words**, written **p(word)**. Its values are 0.5 for done, 0.1 each for dune, dean and Don, and 0.2 for Dan.
children: These probabilities add to one. The largest value is assigned to done, so that is the network’s decision in the example.

teaching.text: **A valid probability distribution can still give the wrong answer.** The input’s low F1 and high F2 support dean, but the largest output probability favors done. The random weights allow processing without supplying useful vowel knowledge.

The correct answer can be represented by **0, 0, 1, 0, 0** in the output order done, dune, dean, Don and Dan. The single one identifies dean; the zeros identify the alternatives that are not the target.

**Stochastic gradient descent** changes the weights gradually using the mismatch between the predicted output and the target. The goal is for a later forward pass on this formant pattern to assign more probability to dean.
children: The formant input and the correct label supply the training example. Learning improves the network’s weights rather than changing the correct label to agree with its initial decision.

coverage.idea: Forward propagation passes activations through successive weighted layers
The displayed p(word) values are a valid probability distribution
The example distribution favors the wrong vowel
A one-hot target identifies dean in the fixed output order
SGD uses target mismatch to improve the weights

teaching.text: **PyTorch** provides tools for specifying this network in Python. **import torch** loads the library, and **import torch.nn as nn** makes its neural-network components available under the shorter name **nn**.
**nn.Sequential** arranges the processing layers in order. The output of one layer becomes the input to the next, matching the forward flow through the network.

**nn.Linear(2, 3)** receives two values and produces three. The next lines convert three to two, two to four and four to five. These numbers describe the layer widths, not the particular formant values.
children: Each output size must match the following layer’s input size. The four Linear lines specify the three hidden layers and the final output layer; the two-value input is received rather than specified as its own Linear processing line.

teaching.text: A **Linear** layer forms weighted sums, the inner products of its inputs with its weights. A **bias** is an extra added constant. **bias=False** removes that constant, and no activation functions are inserted, keeping this network purely linear.
children: A **weight matrix** has one row for each receiving neuron and one column for each incoming value. For **Linear(2, 3)**, three receiving neurons each need weights for the two inputs, so the matrix has **three rows and two columns**.

teaching.text: **Declaring a network is different from training it.** These lines specify its structure and processing order. They do not load vowel examples, compare outputs with targets or update the weights, so the declaration by itself has not learned the vowel categories.

coverage.idea: PyTorch imports make neural-network components available
Sequential specifies the processing order
Linear input/output sizes reproduce the network widths
Linear weighted sums and bias=False define the processing
The shown declaration contains no training procedure
Weight-matrix rows count receiving neurons and columns count incoming values
